newsitem.title: UK: BAA price cap leaves it 150 mln stg short.
newsitem.headline: BAA price cap leaves it 150 mln stg short.

text.p: British airports operator BAA Plc said Thursday the state's new formula capping user charges at its London airports from next year will require it to make up a 150 million stg shortfall in regulated revenue over five years.
Finance director Russell Walls told a news conference that BAA would be seeking ways to both further improve retail revenues and to cut costs over and above its existing plans.
"We will clearly be looking at both (boosting sales and cutting costs)," he said.
"It's challenging because we asked for RPI minus zero and we are getting RPI minus three," he said.
It was too early to say how much of the shortfall would have to be made up from cost cutting rather than increased revenues but there was no immediate threat for jobs, he said.

Walls said the task was challenging but he noted that regulated charges at BAA's three London airports amount to some 360 million stg a year, accounting for only 28 percent of the group's total revenues, of 1,253 million stg last year.

Retail income was up 10.5 percent last year at 556 million stg, making airport shopping BAA's biggest single earner, and he said that figure was set to grow following a share expansion in shopping facilities at BAA's seven British airports.

Walls said another 200,000 square feet of retail space was likely to be added over the next five years but the main expansion programme was complete and the task now was to get passengers to spend more through new marketing initiatives.
Overall retail sales were up by over 10 percent in the first quarter this year with spend per passenger up by over 7.5 percent, he said.
BAA would be revealing whether that trend continued in the second quarter to end-September when it reports half-year results on November 11.
"We are always growing our retail side of the business and it won't be long before retail accounts for more than 50 percent of our business," he said on Thursday.
The CAA's five-yearly pricing review was instituted to regulate landing and passenger handling charges at Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted airports when BAA was privatised in 1987.

The Civil Aviation Authority announced earlier that landing and passenger handling charges must be cut each year at London Heathrow and Gatwick airports by a combined three percentage points below inflation for five years from April 1997.
Prices at the much smaller London Stansted can be raised by one percentage point above the UK's official Retail Price Index (RPI) measure of inflation.

The regime could have been tougher but BAA and the CAA said the formula agreed was designed to anticipate BAA's capital expenditure programme which envisages a giant fifth terminal at Heathrow costing over 1,500 million stg as well as nearly three billion stg of other capital spending over the next 10 years.
The CAA said that most airlines consulted had agreed with the RPI minus three formula.
"The airlines all supported this (agreed) formula because when it came to the crunch they all want this infrastrucutre investment," said Des Wilson, BAA's director of public affairs.
BAA says it does not now expect a government decision on Terminal Five before 1999, since the public planning inquiry hearings are likely to run on until the end of 1997.
But Walls denied suggestions by some airlines that the RPI minus three formula amounted to providing "pre-funding" for Terminal Five.

He said BAA will already have spent around 180 million stg on preparatory work by the end of March next year, with a further 70 million stg likely to be needed before the government of the day gives its ruling.
"We are spending at a rate of about 30 to 40 million stg a year," he said.
-- Greg Mahlich, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
